title: Loading every format
summary: Search can only find what was loaded, and only as well as it was loaded. Nimbus's knowledge lives in Markdown, PDFs with tables, web pages, a menu CSV, order records in JSON, a Word contract, an Excel workbook, a slide deck with speaker notes, an email with an attachment, and code. Module 1's loaders read five of those formats. This module loads all of them **with their structure**: rows keep their column names, tables stay tables, sections keep their headings, slides keep their speaker notes. Then it measures what that does to the 45 evaluation questions.
learn: **Documents and metadata**: text, facts about the text, and stable ids so re-indexing never duplicates
**Text, CSV and JSON**: one Document per file, row or record, and why the phrasing of structured data decides what search finds
**HTML**: keep the main content, drop menus and footers, keep headings; fetch pages with WebBaseLoader
**PDF text and tables**: pages, repeated headers and footers, and tables as Markdown rows instead of loose numbers
**Word, Excel, PowerPoint and email**: sections, rows with headers, speaker notes, quoted replies and attachments
**Custom loaders**: your own sources with `BaseLoader`, streaming with `lazy_load`, and one loader for a whole folder
flow:
data/nimbus/  ─discover─→  loader_for(file) by extension
   .md .txt .html .py ─→ TextFileLoader      one Document per file
   .pdf               ─→ PdfLoader           one per page, tables as Markdown
   .csv               ─→ CsvLoader           one per row, values labelled
   .json              ─→ JsonLoader          one per record, readable lines
   .docx              ─→ DocxLoader          one per section, tables as Markdown
   .xlsx              ─→ XlsxLoader          one per row, header found
   .pptx              ─→ PptxLoader          one per slide + speaker notes
   .eml               ─→ EmlLoader           body without quotes + attachments
   .png               ─→ (Module 3: OCR)     reported as unsupported, never silently skipped

labs.explain:
Every loader produces **Documents**: `page_content` (embedded and searched), `metadata` (facts about the text, used to filter, cite and manage) and an `id`.

The lab gives the handbook a designed set of metadata, splits it, and indexes it three times (first run, an unchanged re-run, a run after one edit) with **random ids** and with **stable ids** built from a hash of the source and text. Count the rows each leaves behind.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: A content hash: the same chunk always gets the same id.

notes.text: Source + text in, the same 16-hex id out, on every machine and every run.

code.why: Production: LangChain's indexing API with a record manager.

notes.text: Chunk identity = hash of content + metadata.
All chunks of a file share a source id, so chunks that disappeared from a file get deleted.

labs.explain:
**TextLoader** reads a file as one Document, **CSVLoader** makes one per row, **DirectoryLoader** loads a folder, and `lazy_load()` streams them. JSON has no single right loader: you decide how a record reads as text.

The lab writes the 12 support orders three ways (**raw JSON**, **labelled `key: value` lines**, and **a written sentence**) and searches for them among every other chunk with six questions. The phrasing changes what gets found.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: Production: one Document per row, every value labelled.

notes.match: text = "\n".join(f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in row.items())
notes.text: Column names travel with the values: '220' alone means nothing.

code.why: Production: a JSON record as readable lines.

notes.text: order_id → 'order id': closer to how people ask.
Nested items flattened to 'name: …, qty: …' instead of JSON.

labs.explain:
A web page is mostly furniture: menus, banners, footers, scripts. **BSHTMLLoader** keeps all visible text; keeping only `<main>` drops the clutter; writing headings as Markdown lets the splitter cut at sections. **WebBaseLoader** fetches pages over HTTP (from a local server here, so no internet is needed).

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

notes.text: The tags that hold site furniture, removed before extracting text.

notes.match: root = soup.find("main") or soup.body or soup
notes.text: Prefer <main>: the page's own content.

labs.explain:
PDFs store text in drawing order, with running headers and footers on every page, and tables as positioned words. The lab extracts page 2 of the annual report (a revenue table) three ways: **plain text**, **pdfplumber's table rows as Markdown**, and **PyMuPDF4LLM** (production). Then it gives the model the last rows of the table as a chunk, **flattened** and **as Markdown**, and asks for a 2024 figure.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: Production: PyMuPDF4LLM, one Markdown Document per page.

notes.text: Tables come out as Markdown tables; headings as #.

code.why: Production: running headers and footers removed per file.

notes.text: A line on most pages of a file is furniture, not content.

code.why: A table as its own Document with element=table.

labs.explain:
Contracts in Word, numbers in Excel, plans in PowerPoint, decisions in email. Quick loaders flatten them: table cells on separate lines, values without their column names, slides without speaker notes, an email with the whole quoted thread. The lab loads the four office files **quickly** and **with structure**, then searches both with the 8 evaluation questions those files answer.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: One Document per section, tables as Markdown.

notes.text: Paragraphs AND tables in document order: that's how a table stays inside its section.
A heading starts a new section.

code.why: One Document per row, cells labelled.

notes.text: Formula results, not formulas.
Read-only workbooks keep the file open until closed.
Speaker notes: what the presenter said, often the detail people ask about.
The quoted thread is cut: it's indexed from its own email.

notes.match: for number, attachment in enumerate(mail.iter_attachments(), start=2):
notes.text: Each attachment becomes its own Document, with the email's headers.

labs.explain:
Your data also lives in APIs, databases and queues. Subclass **BaseLoader**, implement `lazy_load()`, and every LangChain component can use it. The lab streams a large custom source with `load()` and with `lazy_load()` and measures peak memory, then runs production's folder loader over the whole data folder.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: Production's folder loader: the right loader per extension.

notes.text: One registry: adding a format is one line here and one loader class.

code.why: Every file, in a stable order; unsupported files reported.

notes.text: v1 (Module 1) and v2 (this module) side by side, so they can be compared.

path.title: Production path: Nimbus loaders v2
path.summary: Production ingestion goes from five formats to twelve. Every loader keeps the structure a reader relies on, records the same metadata (source, page, file type, plus what's specific: section, sheet, slide, sender), and files no loader can read are reported, never skipped silently. The evaluation step scores v1 against v2 on all 45 questions with the same cleaning, chunking and embeddings.

steps.title: Registry
steps.explain:
`discover()` lists every file (hidden files skipped, stable order) and splits them into supported and unsupported for the chosen version. `loader_for()` maps the extension to a loader. Every loader yields Documents with the same base metadata: `source` (path relative to the data folder: stable across machines), `page` (page, row, record, section or slide number: what a citation points to) and `file_type`.

The version is configuration (`NIMBUS_LOADER_VERSION`), so v1 and v2 can be compared on the same data.

notes.text: Structured formats get their own loader; text-like formats share TextFileLoader.
The version decides which extensions count as supported.
v2 by default; v1 kept for comparison.

production: Unsupported files are logged and listed in the ingestion report: a file nobody can search is a gap to fix, not to hide.
Loaders run per file and a failure is recorded per file: one corrupt spreadsheet must not stop the other 10,000 files.

steps.title: Records
steps.tagline: CSV rows and JSON records as text
steps.explain: Rows and records are embedded as **labelled lines** (`item: Oat Latte`, `price_rupees: 220`), never as raw JSON: the lab measured raw JSON's MRR well below labelled lines on the same 12 orders. Nested values are flattened (`name: Nilgiri Sunrise, qty: 1, price: 720`). Each row or record is its own Document with its row number.

notes.text: The file is closed as soon as its rows are read.

notes.match: records = data if isinstance(data, list) else [data]
notes.text: A list of records → one Document each; any other JSON → one Document.

production: For your most-asked record types (orders, products), a hand-written sentence template is worth adding; keep the generic loader for everything else.
Very large exports (millions of rows) belong in a database the agent queries (Data track), not in a vector index.

steps.title: Office & email
steps.explain: Word documents become one Document per section with tables as Markdown; Excel sheets one per row with the header row found automatically; slides one per slide with speaker notes; emails the new text (quoted replies cut) plus each text attachment. Each carries its own metadata (`section`, `sheet`/`row`, `slide`/`title`, `from`/`subject`/`date`).

code.why: Tables as Markdown: the header row travels with the rows.

production: Binary email attachments (PDFs, images) should go through their own loaders with the email's metadata; here they're skipped and that's visible in the code.
LangChain's Unstructured loaders cover these formats too, at the cost of a large dependency; the small libraries used here are enough for well-formed files.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.tagline: v1 vs v2 on all 45 questions
steps.explain:
Same cleaning, same chunking (500/80), same embeddings: only the loaders differ. The scorecard counts files indexed, questions whose file is indexed (coverage), questions some chunk can answer (answerable), and hit@k and MRR over all 45 questions, plus hit@k on reachable questions only (the retriever's own quality).

Measured: v2 indexes 7 more files, answerable goes 0.64 → 0.91 and hit@5 0.56 → 0.69. The retriever's hit rate on reachable questions falls (0.86 → 0.76) because the new files add harder questions and 38 more chunks compete: that's the next modules' job.

code.why: Both versions through the same evaluation.

notes.text: Which files are indexed decides coverage: a question about an unindexed file can't be found.

production: Run this evaluation whenever a loader changes: a loader bug shows up as answerable dropping, long before users notice.
Track answerable and hit_reachable separately: the first is a loading problem, the second a retrieval problem.
